interview.question: What is IsRestoringProvider?
interview.answer: It is a Solid context provider whose value has type `Accessor<boolean>`. Its purpose is to expose whether a persisted query client is currently being restored.
interview.followUp: How is the value normally populated? `PersistQueryClientProvider` uses this provider to publish the restore state.

interview.question: How is the provider consumed?
interview.answer: The provider communicates restoration status to descendants through context. `useIsRestoring` reads that status, while query APIs also check it internally.
interview.followUp: Why does that internal check matter? It helps prevent race conditions between restoring persisted state and mounting queries.

interview.question: What is its type and declaration?
interview.answer: The documented declaration is `const IsRestoringProvider: ContextProviderComponent<Accessor<boolean>> = IsRestoringContext.Provider;`. Therefore, the supplied value is a Solid accessor returning a boolean.
interview.followUp: What should the accessor return? It should be true during persisted-client restoration and false once restoration has finished.

keyPoints: The exported value is the Solid context provider, typed to accept an accessor of boolean state.
PersistQueryClientProvider uses it to publish restoration status to the query context.
Its boolean state represents whether persisted query-client restoration is in progress.
The companion useIsRestoring primitive is the documented consumer for this context.
gotchas: This provider is generally supplied by PersistQueryClientProvider; manually replacing it means your value must accurately represent the active restore operation.
Consumers should read the context through useIsRestoring rather than depending on the provider object directly.

keepPreviousData.summary: Keeps a query's previous result visible as placeholder data while a changed query key fetches its new result. Pass the function to placeholderData.
keepPreviousData.explanation: keepPreviousData is a generic identity function intended for a query's placeholderData option. When the query key changes, it returns the prior result so the UI can continue displaying it until the replacement data arrives.
keepPreviousData.syntax: function keepPreviousData<T>(previousData: T | undefined): T | undefined;

parameters.name: previousData
parameters.description: Data associated with the previous query key, supplied by the observer; it may be undefined.

keepPreviousData.returns: The previous data unchanged, or undefined when no previous data is available.

example.title: Keep paginated data visible
example.explanation: Passing keepPreviousData as placeholderData preserves the prior result while the query for the changed key is fetching.

useCases.title: Paginated results
useCases.scenario: A page number is included in queryKey and users should not see the list disappear between page requests.

useCases.title: Key-based transitions
useCases.scenario: Filters or another key component changes and the replacement request should transition without an empty intermediate view.

interview.question: What does keepPreviousData accept and return?
interview.answer: keepPreviousData has the signature keepPreviousData<T>(previousData: T | undefined): T | undefined. It receives the prior query-key data from the observer and returns that value unchanged.
interview.followUp: What happens if no prior result exists? The function returns undefined, so the query has no previous data to display.

interview.question: How is keepPreviousData used with a changing query key?
interview.answer: Pass it as the query's placeholderData option. When a key changes, the previous result remains visible instead of the data becoming undefined while the new request runs.
interview.followUp: Why is the query key still significant? A changed key still identifies and fetches distinct query data; keepPreviousData only bridges the display during the transition.

interview.question: What user-interface problem does this function solve?
interview.answer: It is useful for paginated queries whose page number is part of queryKey. The old page can remain rendered until the newly requested page arrives.
interview.followUp: How can an application distinguish transitional data? Track the query's fetching state alongside the displayed data, rather than assuming the retained result is current.

keyPoints: Use the function directly as placeholderData, rather than invoking it yourself.
A changed query key can retain the previous result during the replacement fetch.
The previous query-key result is supplied to the function by the observer.
The return value is the same previous data, with no transformation.
Its generic signature permits any result type and also accounts for an absent previous result.
gotchas: It does not make the new query resolve immediately; it only supplies the previous result as placeholder data during the fetch.

lazyRouteComponent.summary: Creates a one-off, code-split TanStack Router route component. The returned lazy component can be preloaded, and an optional export name supports named exports.
lazyRouteComponent.explanation: Pass an importer that resolves to a module containing the route component. The function returns a React.lazy component and adds a preload method, while an optional export name selects a named export instead of the module's default export.

parameters.name: importer
parameters.description: Function returning a promise that resolves to an object containing the component.

parameters.name: exportName
parameters.description: Optional exported component name; defaults to the default export.

lazyRouteComponent.returns: A React.lazy component that can be preloaded using component.preload().

example.title: Lazy-load a route component
example.explanation: The route loads its default-exported component on demand, splitting the route component into a separate bundle.

useCases.title: Route-level code splitting
useCases.scenario: A route component should be downloaded only when its route is needed.

useCases.title: Preloading a future route
useCases.scenario: Navigation or interaction can begin loading a route before rendering it.

useCases.title: Named component exports
useCases.scenario: The component is exported by name rather than as the module default.

interview.question: What arguments does lazyRouteComponent accept?
interview.answer: It accepts an importer and an optional exportName. The importer must return a promise resolving to a module containing the component; exportName identifies which export to use and defaults to the default export.
interview.followUp: How can the resulting component be loaded before rendering? Call its preload() method, which is exposed on the returned lazy component.

interview.question: What does lazyRouteComponent return?
interview.answer: It creates a one-off code-split route component. The returned value is a React.lazy component that supports preloading through component.preload().
interview.followUp: When should this helper generally be avoided? In file-based routing, use createLazyFileRoute instead.

interview.question: How do you lazy-load a named component export?
interview.answer: Use the default form when the module's component is the default export. Pass the export's name as the second argument when the component is exported by name.
interview.followUp: What must the first argument provide? A function returning a promise for an object that contains the component to load.

keyPoints: It is intended for one-off route-level code splitting and exposes preload() for warming the component before navigation.
The importer is a required function whose promise resolves to a module-like object containing the component.
The optional exportName chooses the component property from the imported module.
The result is a React.lazy component with a preload() method.
gotchas: For file-based routing, prefer createLazyFileRoute rather than using this one-off component helper.
If exportName is omitted, the imported module's default export is used.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Optional route origin used when resolving relative links.

parameters.name: preload
parameters.description: Controls when route data is preloaded.

Link.returns: An anchor element that can be used to navigate to a new location.

example.title: Typed route link
example.explanation: This renders a typed anchor that navigates to a route with a path parameter and updates search parameters.

interview.question: What does the Link component render and why is that useful?
interview.answer: Link renders an actual anchor with a valid href, so users can click it or open it with modifier keys. It also supplies TanStack Router's typed navigation options for route-aware navigation.
interview.followUp: When should useNavigate be preferred? Use it when navigation must happen imperatively as a side effect; otherwise, the Link component is generally preferred.

interview.question: Which navigation data can Link express?
interview.answer: The destination can include a pathname, route parameters, search parameters, hash, and location state. Route parameters are passed through the params option, while search can be an object or a function derived from previous values.
interview.followUp: How can a link preserve existing search parameters? Pass search={true}, or return the previous search object from a functional search option.

interview.question: How does Link preloading work?
interview.answer: Link supports four preload modes: false, intent, viewport, and render. Intent preloads on focus, hover, or touch; viewport preloads when entering the viewport; render preloads immediately after rendering.
interview.followUp: What is a practical conservative default? Keep automatic preloading disabled with false when prefetching is not wanted.

keyPoints: Use Link for declarative navigation between locations in a TanStack Router application.
A link can describe changes to the pathname, query string, hash, and navigation state.
The component outputs a real anchor and href, retaining standard browser link behavior.
Normal anchor attributes, including target, can be used for browser behaviors such as opening a new window.
activeProps and inactiveProps allow link properties to vary according to whether the destination is active.
Preloading can be configured with false, intent, viewport, or render.
gotchas: Route parameter values containing characters such as @ are encoded by default, so the resulting URL may differ from the raw value.
Relative navigation depends on the supplied from route; without it, relative paths resolve from the current active location.
The path-parameter character setting must be chosen when creating the router and cannot be modified afterward.

matchQuery.explanation: matchQuery evaluates one Query against a QueryFilters object. Every supplied filter must match; omitted filters do not constrain the result, and the function returns a boolean.

parameters.name: filters
parameters.description: Filters used to test the query; supported properties include exact, fetchStatus, predicate, queryKey, stale, and type.

parameters.name: query
parameters.description: The query to evaluate against the filters.

matchQuery.returns: boolean — true if the query matches every specified filter.

example.title: Check a query key
example.explanation: Pass a QueryFilters object and a Query instance to test whether the query satisfies every specified filter.

interview.question: What does matchQuery do?
interview.answer: matchQuery accepts QueryFilters and a Query, then returns true only when the query satisfies every specified filter. Unspecified filters are ignored.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect a cache for matches? Retrieve all queries from the QueryCache and filter them with matchQuery.

interview.question: How do queryKey and exact affect matching?
interview.answer: Set queryKey in the filters to test the query key. The exact option controls whether the key must match exactly rather than using a matching prefix.
interview.followUp: What other query-selection dimensions are available? Use type, stale, fetchStatus, or predicate filters.

interview.question: What are the inputs and output of matchQuery?
interview.answer: The function returns a boolean indicating whether the query matches all requested criteria. Its second argument is a Query instance, not a query key or query data object.
interview.followUp: How would you select only active stale queries? Provide type: 'active' and stale: true in the filters.

keyPoints: Use matchQuery to evaluate a Query against a QueryFilters object.
The exact filter requires an exact query-key match.
fetchStatus can select queries that are fetching, paused, or idle.
predicate provides custom matching logic based on the Query object.
queryKey restricts matching to a specified key or tuple prefix.
stale selects whether stale queries should match.
type limits matching to active, inactive, or all queries.
gotchas: All supplied filters are combined as required conditions; leaving a filter out removes that condition.

MutationCache.summary: MutationCache stores mutations and is normally accessed through QueryClient. It supports inspecting, filtering, clearing, and subscribing to mutation-cache updates.
MutationCache.explanation: MutationCache stores mutation instances and is normally managed through QueryClient rather than accessed directly. You can inspect all or filtered mutations, remove everything, or subscribe to notifications about mutations being added, removed, or updated.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Optional configuration used to initialize the cache.

MutationCache.returns: A MutationCache instance from the constructor; getAll() returns all mutations, find() returns a matching mutation or undefined, findAll() returns matching mutations, and subscribe() returns an unsubscribe function.

example.title: Inspect and observe a mutation cache
example.explanation: Obtains the client-owned cache, observes cache notifications, and filters mutations by pending status.

useCases.title: Monitor cache notifications
useCases.scenario: Observe application-wide mutation activity for logging, metrics, or debugging.

useCases.title: Query mutation state
useCases.scenario: Inspect mutations currently waiting to finish or matching a mutation key.

useCases.title: Clear mutation storage
useCases.scenario: Remove all stored mutation instances when resetting client state.

interview.question: What is MutationCache and how is it normally accessed?
interview.answer: MutationCache is the storage for mutations and is owned by QueryClient. A client creates a default cache unless one is supplied, and getMutationCache() returns the connected instance.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect only pending mutations? Call getMutationCache().findAll({ status: 'pending' }); it returns the mutations matching those filters.

interview.question: How do the cache inspection methods differ?
interview.answer: getAll() returns every mutation currently held by the cache. find() retrieves one matching mutation, while findAll() retrieves all matching mutations.
interview.followUp: What should code expect when no mutation matches? find() yields undefined, whereas findAll() yields an empty array.

interview.question: How can code observe and reset MutationCache?
interview.answer: subscribe() registers a listener for cache notifications, including mutations being added, removed, or updated. It returns an unsubscribe function that stops that listener.
interview.followUp: How can a cache be reset completely? Call clear(), which removes all mutations from the cache.

keyPoints: It is the cache layer that holds mutation instances.
Subscriptions report recognized cache changes through the inherited Subscribable mechanism.
Relevant notifications include mutation additions, removals, and updates.
The constructor accepts an optional MutationCacheConfig and returns a new MutationCache.
clear() empties the cache completely.
getAll() provides the complete collection of stored mutations.
subscribe() registers a callback for each update the cache reports.
gotchas: Prefer QueryClient for ordinary mutation-cache interaction; direct access is intended for specialized inspection or cache-level behavior.
Always retain and invoke the function returned by subscribe when the observer is no longer needed.

notFound.summary: Creates a TanStack Router not-found error for missing resources or route handling. Return it or throw it from beforeLoad or loader callbacks, with options available to select handling and control throwing.
notFound.explanation: Call notFound to create a TanStack Router not-found error. Throw it from a route loader or beforeLoad callback when a resource is absent; alternatively, configure options such as routeId, data, or throw to control handling and whether the function throws immediately.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional configuration for the not-found error, including throw, routeId, and data.

notFound.returns: A NotFoundError object by default; with options.throw set to true, the function throws the object instead.

example.title: Throw from a route loader
example.explanation: The loader throws a not-found error when the requested post does not exist.

useCases.title: Signal a missing resource
useCases.scenario: A route loader cannot retrieve a post, user, or other resource by identifier.

useCases.title: Force immediate throwing
useCases.scenario: A helper needs to throw immediately rather than return an error object.

useCases.title: Select the handling route
useCases.scenario: A specific route or the root route should render the not-found UI.

interview.question: What does notFound do?
interview.answer: notFound creates a NotFoundError that can be returned or thrown from route beforeLoad and loader callbacks. Throwing it signals TanStack Router to render the applicable notFoundComponent.
interview.followUp: How can the root route handle the error? Use routeId for the root route, or configure the router's notFoundMode as root so root handling is selected.

interview.question: How does the throw option change behavior?
interview.answer: Calling notFound() returns the error object by default. Passing { throw: true } makes the function throw the object instead, which is useful when a throwing helper should have a never-like control flow.
interview.followUp: What happens when throw is false or omitted? The object is returned and must be thrown by the caller if it should trigger not-found handling.

interview.question: What is routeId used for?
interview.answer: The optional routeId identifies the route that should attempt to handle the error. If that route has no notFoundComponent, the error can bubble to a parent, eventually reaching the root when needed.
interview.followUp: What is the default handling route? TanStack Router normally tries the route that threw the error, while notFoundMode can change route-matching behavior.

keyPoints: notFound constructs the error representation used by TanStack Router for missing resources.
Use it in route lifecycle callbacks to signal that required data is unavailable.
Its API takes one optional options object.
gotchas: By default, notFound returns an error object; use throw: true when the call itself must throw it.

notifyManager.summary: notifyManager batches TanStack Query updates and schedules notification callbacks. It supports framework-specific batching, custom notification handling, and configurable scheduling.
notifyManager.explanation: notifyManager coordinates TanStack Query notifications by batching updates and scheduling callbacks. Its batch method supports nesting and returns the callback's result, while scheduling defaults to setTimeout and can be customized for framework-specific rendering or test behavior.

parameters.name: batch callback
parameters.description: Callback executed within the batching scope.

parameters.name: schedule callback
parameters.description: Notification callback queued for the next batch.

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: Framework-provided function that batches notifications.

parameters.name: scheduler
parameters.description: Function used to schedule the next batch.

notifyManager.returns: notifyManager is an object exposing batch, schedule, setBatchNotifyFunction, setNotifyFunction, and setScheduler. batch returns the callback's result; schedule and configuration methods return void.

example.title: Batch and schedule notifications
example.code:
import { notifyManager } from '@tanstack/query-core'

const values: number[] = []

notifyManager.batch(() => {
  values.push(1)
  notifyManager.schedule(() => values.push(2))
})

console.log(values)
example.explanation: Runs a synchronous update inside a batch and schedules another callback for the next notification batch.

useCases.title: Batch query updates
useCases.scenario: Reduce redundant subscriber work when several query updates occur together.

useCases.title: Framework rendering integration
useCases.scenario: Connect TanStack Query to a framework's own batching primitive.

useCases.title: Test-safe notifications
useCases.scenario: Wrap notifications with a testing utility such as React.act.

useCases.title: Control notification timing
useCases.scenario: Run notification batches in a microtask, animation frame, or delayed timeout.

interview.question: Why does TanStack Query use notifyManager?
interview.answer: notifyManager batches updates and schedules notification callbacks so multiple changes can be processed together. This reduces redundant subscriber work and, for framework adapters, can prevent multiple renders for one query update.
interview.followUp: How can a framework integrate its own batching primitive? Use setBatchNotifyFunction with the framework's batch function so notifications are grouped into one tick.

interview.question: What are the important semantics of batch?
interview.answer: batch executes updates within a batching scope, and nested scopes defer flushing until the outermost scope ends. It also passes the callback's return value through to the caller.
interview.followUp: What happens to callbacks scheduled during a batch? They are queued for the next batch rather than executed immediately.

interview.question: How can notification timing be customized?
interview.answer: schedule queues a callback for the next batch. By default, the next batch is scheduled with setTimeout(callback, 0), but setScheduler can replace that timing function.
interview.followUp: How would you schedule before the next frame? Configure setScheduler with requestAnimationFrame.

keyPoints: notifyManager is the core utility for coordinating callback scheduling and notification batching.
batch groups updates performed within its callback.
batch preserves and returns the callback's result.
A configured batch notification function groups every callback invocation it wraps.
setBatchNotifyFunction lets framework integrations provide their native batching mechanism.
schedule defers a callback until the next notification batch.
setScheduler changes the function responsible for starting the next batch.
gotchas: Nested batches do not flush independently; queued work waits until the outermost batch completes.
A custom notify function must invoke every callback it receives.
Changing the scheduler changes when the next batch runs; the default is a zero-delay timeout.

onlineManager.explanation: The singleton tracks whether TanStack Query considers the application connected. It normally derives this from browser online and offline events, but you can replace that detection with a custom listener or directly override the state.

parameters.name: setup

onlineManager.returns: Singleton OnlineManager instance; isOnline returns boolean and listener-registration status returns boolean.

example.title: Control the online state

onlineManager.setOnline(false)
console.log(onlineManager.isOnline())
onlineManager.setOnline(true)
example.explanation: Manually toggles TanStack Query's connectivity state and reads it back.

useCases.title: Platform-specific network detection

useCases.title: Manual connectivity control
useCases.scenario: Tests or application infrastructure need to force online or offline behavior.

interview.question: What is onlineManager used for?
interview.answer: onlineManager is the singleton OnlineManager used to manage and observe TanStack Query's online state. It exposes methods for querying the state, overriding it, and installing custom detection.
interview.followUp: How would you support React Native connectivity? Install a platform network listener and pass its connection status to the callback received by setEventListener.

interview.question: How do you read the current online state?
interview.answer: Call onlineManager.isOnline() to read the current status. It returns a boolean, with true meaning TanStack Query currently considers the app online.
interview.followUp: What should code do when the status changes? Use setOnline through the configured listener so TanStack Query receives each new boolean state.

interview.question: How can custom connectivity detection be configured?
interview.answer: Use onlineManager.setEventListener to replace the default browser event handling. Its setup function receives setOnline, and the setup function should return cleanup for the installed listener.
interview.followUp: When is direct setOnline useful? It is useful when application code already knows connectivity or must manually force the state during testing or specialized runtime integration.

keyPoints: The object centralizes the connectivity state consumed by TanStack Query.
In a browser, its default detector responds to window connectivity events.
Call isOnline when code needs the current connectivity decision.
Use setOnline to explicitly mark the application online or offline.
Use setEventListener when the default browser detector does not match the runtime.
The listener-registration status method reports whether listeners remain active.
gotchas: The initial assumption is that the application is online until connectivity detection changes it.
A custom event listener must invoke the supplied callback whenever connectivity changes.

Outlet.summary: TanStack Router's Outlet renders the next matching child route inside a parent route component. It takes no props and renders null when no child route matches.
Outlet.explanation: Outlet is a parameterless component for nested TanStack Router layouts. When rendered inside a route component, it inserts the next matching child route at that position; with no matching child, it renders nothing.
Outlet.returns: The matched child route's component, errorComponent, pendingComponent, or notFoundComponent; otherwise null.

example.explanation: Renders the root layout and places the currently matched child route where Outlet appears.

useCases.title: Place child pages inside a parent route's persistent layout.
useCases.scenario: Nested layouts

useCases.title: Wrap protected child routes in a layout or pathless layout route.

useCases.title: Allow the matched child component, pending UI, error UI, or not-found UI to render at the nested position.

interview.question: What is Outlet used for, and what does it render?
interview.answer: Outlet renders the next potentially matching child route inside a parent route's component tree. It accepts no props, and it renders null when no child route matches.
interview.followUp: What happens if a route has no component? TanStack Router renders an Outlet automatically for that route.

interview.question: How does Outlet support nested layouts?
interview.answer: Place Outlet anywhere in the parent route component tree where the child route should appear. The surrounding elements remain part of the parent layout while the matched child is inserted at that location.
interview.followUp: How would you create a shared authenticated layout? Use a layout or pathless layout route, render the shared UI around Outlet, and perform the authentication check in beforeLoad.

interview.question: What does Outlet return for matched and unmatched children?
interview.answer: The component renders the matched child route's component, error component, pending component, or not-found component as appropriate. It has no configurable props.
interview.followUp: What is the fallback when no child route matches? Outlet returns null, so any fallback UI must be supplied by the surrounding route component.

keyPoints: Outlet inserts the next child route that can match the current location.
It has no props and may be placed at any point in the parent route's component tree.
For a matched child, Outlet selects the applicable component state, including normal, error, pending, or not-found rendering.
When no child route matches, Outlet contributes no rendered output.
Outlet is the rendering mechanism that makes nested route composition possible.
gotchas: An Outlet does not render fallback content when its parent has no matching child route; it produces null.
A route without its own component receives Outlet behavior automatically, so adding a component is only necessary when defining layout content.

PaginationState.explanation: PaginationState is the feature-specific state shape for TanStack Table pagination. It stores the currently selected zero-based page through pageIndex and the number of rows requested per page through pageSize, and can be used for local state or external atoms.

interview.question: What does PaginationState contain?
interview.answer: PaginationState is the state object used for table pagination. Its pageIndex is zero-based, and pageSize specifies how many rows belong to a page.
interview.followUp: How would you use it with server-side fetching? Include the pagination object in the query key and use it to request the corresponding page and size.

interview.question: When should you use PaginationState instead of a broader table-state type?
interview.answer: Use PaginationState when creating local state or an external atom for only the pagination slice. The documentation recommends feature-specific state types such as PaginationState for that purpose.
interview.followUp: Why prefer the feature-specific type? It keeps the state contract narrow and aligned with the table feature being controlled.

interview.question: Why control PaginationState outside the table?
interview.answer: The state can be controlled externally and supplied back to the table, allowing another owner to react to pagination changes. This is useful when pagination must also drive data fetching.
interview.followUp: What should a server-side result provide alongside the requested rows? Return the rows for the requested page and the total row count so the table can derive pagination information.

keyPoints: pageIndex identifies the selected page using zero-based indexing.
pageSize records how many rows the current pagination configuration requests per page.
Use PaginationState when defining local state or an external atom for the pagination slice.
The same state shape applies with either client-side pagination or manually fetched server-side pages.
gotchas: It is an object with exactly the documented pagination properties, pageIndex and pageSize; do not treat it as a numeric page value.
pageIndex starts at 0 for the first page, so UI page numbers may need a +1 conversion.
When a query key or other external consumer needs pagination, keep the slice in external state rather than assuming the table instance is the only source.

placeholderData.summary: placeholderData lets a query render with temporary data while the real request runs. Unlike initialData, the temporary value is not persisted in the cache and is marked with isPlaceholderData.
placeholderData.explanation: placeholderData supplies observer-level temporary data so a query can render successfully while its request runs. The temporary value is not written to the cache; the result exposes isPlaceholderData so the UI can distinguish it from fetched data.

parameters.name: placeholderData
parameters.type: TData | ((previousData: TData | undefined, previousQuery: Query) => TData)
parameters.description: A temporary value or function producing temporary query data; it is used while the real data is fetched and is not persisted in the cache.

placeholderData.returns: A query result containing the temporary data, with isPlaceholderData set to true while that data is displayed; the fetched result replaces it when available.

example.title: Render with placeholder data
example.explanation: The component renders immediately with temporary todo data while the real response is fetched in the background.

useCases.title: Progressive rendering
useCases.scenario: A list has enough summary fields to render rows before detail requests finish.

useCases.title: Lagged pagination
useCases.scenario: A page-number query changes keys and should keep the previous page visible during refetching.

useCases.title: Stable UI shape
useCases.scenario: A skeleton or lightweight fake object can provide the shape required by the view immediately.

interview.question: What does placeholderData do, and how does it differ from initialData?
interview.answer: placeholderData makes a query behave as though it already has data while the actual request proceeds. Unlike initialData, the supplied value is not persisted to the cache.
interview.followUp: How can the UI identify the temporary state? Check the result's isPlaceholderData flag, which is true while placeholder data is being supplied.

interview.question: What query status should you expect when placeholderData is present?
interview.answer: A query using placeholderData starts in the success state rather than pending because it has displayable data. The real fetch still runs in the background and replaces the temporary result when it completes.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful for loading states? It allows partial or fake data to render without showing an empty pending view.

interview.question: What can a placeholderData function access?
interview.answer: placeholderData may be a function. That function can receive data and query metadata from a previous successful query, enabling the prior result to remain visible during a key change.
interview.followUp: What common pagination pattern follows from this? Return previousData from the placeholder function so old results remain visible until the new page arrives.

keyPoints: Temporary data affects the displayed query result but is not stored as cached query state.
It is useful when partial or synthetic values can support an immediate, usable render.
Configure placeholderData declaratively on a query when an immediate provisional result is needed.
The query avoids the pending state because placeholder content is available from the start.
The initial result reports success even though the displayed value is only provisional.
A function form supports dynamic placeholders rather than one fixed value.
The function can inspect the previous successful query's data and metadata, supporting smooth transitions between query keys.
gotchas: Do not treat placeholderData as cached data: it only affects the current query result and does not populate the query cache.
Use isPlaceholderData to avoid treating the temporary value as the completed server response.

QueryCache.summary: QueryCache stores TanStack Query's query data, metadata, and state. It supports creating, finding, clearing, and observing cached queries, but applications normally use QueryClient instead.
QueryCache.explanation: QueryCache is TanStack Query's storage layer for query data, metadata, and state. It can be constructed with configuration, queried synchronously, cleared, or observed for tracked cache changes, although most application code should use QueryClient instead.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Optional configuration for cache behavior and callbacks.

QueryCache.returns: A QueryCache instance; build returns an existing or newly created Query, while subscription methods provide an unsubscribe function.

example.title: Create and observe a QueryCache
example.explanation: Creates a cache with an error callback, observes cache events, clears it, and then removes the subscription.

useCases.scenario: Cache inspection

useCases.scenario: Cache lifecycle

useCases.title: Observe tracked additions, removals, and updates
useCases.scenario: Instrumentation

useCases.title: Create or retrieve Query instances for framework integrations and plugins
useCases.scenario: Core integrations

interview.question: What is QueryCache responsible for, and how is it normally accessed?
interview.answer: QueryCache stores the data, metadata, and state for the queries it contains. QueryClient is normally the application-facing interface for working with a specific cache.
interview.followUp: How can an application observe cache changes? Use subscribe; it reports safe, tracked updates such as queries being added, removed, or updated.

interview.question: How is a QueryCache created and what operations does it provide?
interview.answer: The constructor accepts an optional QueryCacheConfig object. The cache can then expose operations such as build, find, findAll, clear, and subscribe.
interview.followUp: What does build do when the requested query is absent? It creates a Query instance and adds it to the cache.

interview.question: What does QueryCache.build do?
interview.answer: build checks the supplied query options' queryKey or queryHash. It returns the existing matching Query, or creates and stores a new one when no match exists.
interview.followUp: Why might direct QueryCache access be inappropriate for UI code? QueryClient and framework integrations provide the intended higher-level interaction model.

keyPoints: It is the core storage mechanism behind TanStack Query's cached queries.
Each contained query contributes its data, metadata, and state to the cache.
Subscriptions provide notifications for tracked cache updates.
Typical subscription events include query creation, removal, and updates.
Construction optionally accepts QueryCacheConfig and returns a QueryCache instance.
build reuses a matching query or creates and caches one when necessary.
gotchas: Prefer QueryClient for normal application cache operations rather than accessing QueryCache directly.
A subscriber is not notified when query state is mutated outside the cache's tracked mechanisms.

QueryClient.summary: QueryClient is TanStack Query’s imperative interface for interacting with query and mutation caches. It also owns client-level defaults and methods for fetching, reading, updating, and managing cached data.
QueryClient.explanation: QueryClient is the imperative entry point for TanStack Query's query and mutation caches. It owns those caches, applies configured defaults, and exposes operations for fetching, reading, updating, invalidating, refetching, cancelling, or removing cached queries.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Optional configuration containing query and mutation caches plus default options for resources created through the client.

QueryClient.returns: A QueryClient instance that owns query and mutation caches and exposes cache-management methods.

example.title: Fetch and read cached data
example.explanation: Creates a client with a default query freshness period, fetches and caches a query, then synchronously reads its cached data.

useCases.title: Fetch data imperatively
useCases.scenario: A route loader or server-side function needs data before rendering.

useCases.title: Prefetch upcoming data
useCases.scenario: A screen is likely to need data shortly, but should not block the current render.

useCases.title: Manage cache state
useCases.scenario: An event handler must update or invalidate cached resources after a mutation.

interview.question: What is the purpose of QueryClient?
interview.answer: QueryClient provides imperative access to TanStack Query's caches. It owns a QueryCache and MutationCache and stores defaults applied to queries and mutations created through it.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid an unnecessary network request? Use fetchQuery with a suitable staleTime; it returns cached data while that data is still fresh.

interview.question: When would you use fetchQuery instead of getQueryData?
interview.answer: fetchQuery asynchronously fetches and caches a query, returning its data or throwing an error. If matching cached data is not stale according to staleTime, it returns that cached value instead of fetching.
interview.followUp: How does this differ from prefetchQuery? prefetchQuery performs the fetch without requiring the caller to use the resulting data.

interview.question: What does getQueryData do when no cache entry exists?
interview.answer: getQueryData synchronously reads an existing query's cached data. It only reads the cache and returns undefined when the query is absent.
interview.followUp: How can several cached queries be inspected together? Use getQueriesData with a query key or query filter to obtain matching entries.

keyPoints: Use one QueryClient as the imperative coordinator for query and mutation cache operations.
The client owns both cache types, creating default caches when custom ones are not supplied.
Default options configured on the client affect resources created through that client.
fetchQuery combines retrieval and conditional fetching, based on cache freshness.
getQueryCache exposes the underlying query cache associated with the client.
gotchas: Imperative fetches do not inherit observer retry behavior; configure retry explicitly when using fetchQuery.
getQueryData does not fetch missing data, so callers must handle an undefined result.

QueryClientProvider.summary: QueryClientProvider supplies a QueryClient to a React component tree. It also manages the client's mount and unmount lifecycle.
QueryClientProvider.explanation: QueryClientProvider places the supplied QueryClient into React context so descendant components can retrieve it with useQueryClient. Mounting and unmounting the provider also mounts or unmounts the client, connecting it to focus and online events.

parameters.name: client
parameters.description: The QueryClient instance to provide.

parameters.name: children
parameters.description: The components that get access to the provided QueryClient.

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: A custom React Query context; otherwise the default context is used.

QueryClientProvider.returns: An Element containing the supplied children, with access to the provided QueryClient through context.

example.title: Provide a QueryClient to React components
example.explanation: Creates one client and makes it available to the descendant component tree.

useCases.title: Make one configured QueryClient available throughout the app.
useCases.scenario: Application bootstrap

useCases.title: Allow descendant components to use query and mutation hooks backed by the supplied client.
useCases.scenario: Query hooks

useCases.title: Let the client observe focus and online events while the provider is mounted.
useCases.scenario: Focus and reconnect behavior

interview.question: What problem does QueryClientProvider solve?
interview.answer: QueryClientProvider supplies a QueryClient to descendant components through context. Those components can then retrieve the client with useQueryClient.
interview.followUp: How does the provider affect the client's lifecycle? It calls client.mount() when mounted and client.unmount() when removed, enabling focus and online event subscriptions.

interview.question: What are the important QueryClientProvider props?
interview.answer: The required client prop is the QueryClient instance that the provider exposes. The children receive access to that instance through the provider.
interview.followUp: What happens if a component is outside the provider? It cannot obtain the provider's QueryClient through the normal context-based useQueryClient mechanism.

interview.question: What is the component's API shape?
interview.answer: The React signature is function QueryClientProvider(props: QueryClientProviderProps): Element. Its props include a required client and optional children.
interview.followUp: When might a custom context be relevant? The context prop lets an application use a custom React Query context instead of the default context.

keyPoints: Use the provider at the application boundary to make a QueryClient available to the component tree.
Its two core inputs are the QueryClient to expose and the descendant content that consumes it.
Descendants wrapped by the provider are the components granted access to the supplied client.
The returned element wraps children so hooks such as useQueryClient can read the client.
Provider lifecycle integration lets the client respond to focus and online status changes.
gotchas: The provider manages the client's mount lifecycle, so mounting and unmounting it also changes the client's event subscriptions.
Do not start new code with contextSharing; the documentation marks this option as deprecated.

QueryErrorResetBoundary.summary: QueryErrorResetBoundary scopes query-error resets to a component subtree. Give its render-prop reset function to an error boundary so a retry action can clear query errors before rendering again.
QueryErrorResetBoundary.explanation: QueryErrorResetBoundary provides a reset function to descendant content. Pair that function with a React error boundary so a user-triggered reset clears query errors and allows queries using suspense or throwOnError to try again during a later render.

parameters.name: children
parameters.description: Either rendered content or a function receiving QueryErrorResetBoundaryValue and returning rendered content.

example.title: Retry failed queries from an error boundary
example.explanation: Connects a React error boundary's reset action to TanStack Query's query-error reset function.

useCases.title: Retry suspense queries
useCases.scenario: A suspense query throws into a React error boundary and the fallback offers a retry button.

useCases.title: Recover from thrown query errors
useCases.scenario: Queries configured with throwOnError need coordinated recovery after an error fallback is reset.

useCases.title: Scope recovery to a subtree
useCases.scenario: Several related queries should share a reset lifecycle within one page or widget.

interview.question: What problem does QueryErrorResetBoundary solve?
interview.answer: It is a React component that scopes query-error resetting to its boundary. Its children may be a render function receiving a reset value, which can be passed to an error boundary's onReset callback.
interview.followUp: How does the hook differ? useQueryErrorResetBoundary resets errors in the closest component boundary, or globally when no boundary exists.

interview.question: How is it wired to an error boundary?
interview.answer: Use the component around the content whose query errors should be reset. Render-prop children receive reset, and the error boundary invokes that function when its fallback is reset.
interview.followUp: Why connect onReset rather than only the fallback button? Because the error-boundary reset lifecycle is the event that should coordinate the query reset and the component re-render.

interview.question: What does the children prop accept?
interview.answer: The component's children can be either a plain React node or a function receiving QueryErrorResetBoundaryValue. The rendered result is either returned directly or produced by calling that function.
interview.followUp: What does the value currently expose? The documented example uses its reset function to clear query errors.

keyPoints: Reset behavior is scoped to queries inside the component boundary.
The required children prop supplies the UI contained by the reset boundary.
Children may be a React node or a render function that receives the boundary reset value.
The component renders plain children directly and calls function children with the boundary value.
The component accepts QueryErrorResetBoundaryProps and returns a React Element.
gotchas: Use this boundary when query errors are surfaced through suspense or throwOnError; ordinary rendering does not by itself require this reset coordination.

queryFn.summary: queryFn is the data-fetching function for a TanStack Query. It receives QueryFunctionContext and must return defined data or throw; a configured default can provide it when omitted.
queryFn.explanation: queryFn is the function TanStack Query invokes to obtain data for a query. It receives QueryFunctionContext, including the query key and cancellation signal, and must resolve usable data or throw an error; it may be omitted when a default query function is configured.

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: Context containing the query key, page parameter when applicable, and other query execution context.

queryFn.returns: TQueryFnData or Promise<TQueryFnData>; successful results must be defined, while failures should throw.

example.title: A query function using QueryFunctionContext
example.explanation: The query function receives a context object, uses its abort signal for the request, and resolves parsed data or throws when the response fails.

useCases.title: Network data loading
useCases.scenario: Fetch JSON from an HTTP endpoint and return the parsed response.

useCases.title: Context-aware requests
useCases.scenario: Use query context values to select the resource or pass cancellation to a request.

useCases.title: Default query functions
useCases.scenario: Share a standard fetching implementation through QueryClient defaults.

interview.question: What contract must a queryFn satisfy?
interview.answer: queryFn is the function used to request a query's data. It receives QueryFunctionContext and must return data asynchronously or throw an error; the resolved value must not be undefined.
interview.followUp: What can make queryFn optional? A default query function configured with setQueryDefaults or setDefaultOptions can supply it when the query does not define one.

interview.question: What does queryFn receive?
interview.answer: The function receives QueryFunctionContext rather than only the query key. This context lets the implementation use query metadata such as the key and request cancellation signal.
interview.followUp: How should a fetch-based query function handle cancellation? Pass the context's signal to the request so cancellation can propagate to the underlying fetch.

interview.question: When is queryFn optional?
interview.answer: A queryFn can be supplied directly in query options or inherited from query defaults. The option is required when no default query function is available.
interview.followUp: Does the same rule apply across QueryClient fetching APIs? Query options are shared by observers and QueryClient methods, so the configured query function is used wherever those options apply.

keyPoints: queryFn defines how TanStack Query obtains the query's data.
Its single input is a QueryFunctionContext object.
The function may return the data directly or return a promise of that data.
Defaults configured on the QueryClient can provide the function when an option-level function is absent.
gotchas: Returning undefined or swallowing request failures violates the query function contract; resolve data or throw.
Ensure every successful execution returns a defined value.
A query function is optional only when an applicable default has been configured.

queryKey.summary: queryKey is the array identity for TanStack Query data. It determines cache identity, carries request parameters, and is passed to queryFn through QueryFunctionContext.
queryKey.explanation: A queryKey is an array that names and parameterizes cached query data. TanStack Query hashes it into a stable identity, uses it to distinguish cache entries, and supplies it to the query function so request variables can be derived consistently.
queryKey.syntax: useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos', { status, page }], queryFn: fetchTodoList })

parameters.name: queryKey
parameters.description: The array used to identify and parameterize the query.

queryKey.returns: The page documents queryKey as an option rather than a standalone return value.

example.title: A parameterized todo-list query
example.explanation: The key identifies the requested todo list and is available to the query function through its context.

useCases.title: Parameterize list queries
useCases.scenario: A list endpoint supports filters or pagination.

useCases.title: Identify individual resources
useCases.scenario: A detail endpoint needs an entity identifier.

useCases.title: Share cache entries
useCases.scenario: Several components need the same cached request.

interview.question: What purpose does queryKey serve?
interview.answer: A queryKey is the identity for a query's cached data. TanStack Query hashes it into a stable hash and uses key changes to update the query.
interview.followUp: How can a query function use request parameters? It receives a QueryFunctionContext containing queryKey, so it can destructure variables from the key.

interview.question: How should a key represent a parameterized query?
interview.answer: Include values that distinguish the requested data, such as an item ID or filter and page object. The query function can then read those values from its context instead of closing over them.
interview.followUp: What benefit does this provide for extracted functions? The same function can derive its request entirely from the supplied context.

interview.question: How does queryKey reach queryFn?
interview.answer: The key is passed to the query function as part of QueryFunctionContext. This lets an extracted function read the current key and build the corresponding request.
interview.followUp: What else is in the context? The documentation lists the QueryClient, an AbortSignal, and optional metadata alongside queryKey.

keyPoints: Provide queryKey as the query's identifying array.
TanStack Query converts the key into a stable cache identity.
Keys identify cached data, but they also carry the inputs used by the query function.
The current key is available to queryFn through its context.
QueryFunctionContext includes queryKey as its QueryKey value.
gotchas: Changing the key normally triggers a new query, but this automatic behavior is disabled when enabled is false.

QueryObserver.summary: QueryObserver observes one query and produces a QueryObserverResult from its state. It supports framework adapters and direct, framework-independent subscriptions.
QueryObserver.explanation: QueryObserver connects a QueryClient to one query and turns query state into a QueryObserverResult. It recalculates when the query or observer options change, and subscribers receive notifications when the computed result changes. Use getCurrentResult for a snapshot or subscribe for ongoing updates.
QueryObserver.syntax: new QueryObserver<TQueryFnData, TError, TData, TQueryData, TQueryKey>(client: QueryClient, options: QueryObserverOptions<TQueryFnData, TError, TData, TQueryData, TQueryKey>): QueryObserver<TQueryFnData, TError, TData, TQueryData, TQueryKey>

parameters.name: client
parameters.description: The QueryClient used to access and observe the query cache.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Configuration describing the query and result typing.

QueryObserver.returns: A QueryObserver instance that computes results for and notifies subscribers about one observed query.

example.title: Observe a query outside a framework
example.explanation: Creates a core observer, subscribes to result changes, triggers a fetch, and removes the subscription afterward.

useCases.title: Build query hooks
useCases.scenario: A framework adapter needs a reactive query result.

useCases.title: Observe queries directly
useCases.scenario: A non-framework service needs cache-backed updates.

useCases.title: Switch observed queries
useCases.scenario: A client changes which cached query it tracks.

interview.question: What problem does QueryObserver solve?
interview.answer: QueryObserver watches one query in the QueryCache and computes a QueryObserverResult. It recomputes and notifies subscribers when the query or the observer options change.
interview.followUp: How would you consume a result without subscribing? Call getCurrentResult(), but remember that it returns only the latest point-in-time result.

interview.question: How is a QueryObserver created?
interview.answer: Construct it with a QueryClient and QueryObserverOptions. The options describe the query being observed, and the constructor returns a QueryObserver instance.
interview.followUp: How can the observed query be changed? Update the observer's options with the appropriate inherited option-update mechanism, causing the current query and result to be recalculated.

interview.question: How do you receive updates?
interview.answer: subscribe() registers a listener for observer-result changes and returns an unsubscribe function. Use getCurrentResult() when a synchronous snapshot is sufficient.
interview.followUp: Why should a subscriber be removed? Because the returned unsubscribe function stops future notifications when the consumer no longer needs the observer.

keyPoints: It observes exactly one QueryCache query and exposes a derived QueryObserverResult.
Changes to either the query or observer options trigger result recomputation and possible subscriber notification.
Framework hooks such as useQuery use QueryObserver as their underlying primitive.
The class is also suitable for framework-independent code that observes or switches queries.
getCurrentQuery() identifies the Query currently attached to the observer.
getCurrentResult() returns the latest computed result.
updateResult() recalculates and stores the result using the current query and options.
gotchas: getCurrentResult() is only a snapshot; use subscribe() when the consumer must react to future updates.
Result recomputation does not necessarily notify listeners: notification occurs when the resulting value changes.

queryOptions.summary: queryOptions builds reusable, type-safe TanStack Query configurations. The returned options work with hooks and imperative QueryClient APIs while carrying query data and error types through the query key.
queryOptions.explanation: queryOptions packages a query key and its behavior into a reusable, type-aware options object. Its returned value brands the key with the query function's data and error types, allowing the same configuration to work with hooks and imperative QueryClient methods while preserving inference.
queryOptions.syntax: function queryOptions<TQueryFnData, TError, TData, TQueryKey>(options: DefinedInitialDataOptions<TQueryFnData, TError, TData, TQueryKey>): DefinedInitialDataOptions<TQueryFnData, TError, TData, TQueryKey> & QueryKeyWithDataTag<TQueryKey, TQueryFnData, TError>;

parameters.name: options
parameters.type: DefinedInitialDataOptions<TQueryFnData, TError, TData, TQueryKey> | UnusedSkipTokenOptions<TQueryFnData, TError, TData, TQueryKey> | UndefinedInitialDataOptions<TQueryFnData, TError, TData, TQueryKey>
parameters.description: A query options object, including the required queryKey and the query behavior accepted by useQuery.

queryOptions.returns: The supplied query options augmented with a QueryKeyWithDataTag carrying the query function's data and error types.

example.title: Reusable typed query options
example.explanation: Define one typed options object and reuse it with a query hook or imperative QueryClient API.

useCases.title: Centralize query configuration
useCases.scenario: Several components use the same resource query and should share one cache definition.

useCases.title: Reuse options across APIs
useCases.scenario: A feature needs both a React hook and an imperative QueryClient operation.

useCases.title: Preserve type inference
useCases.scenario: A TypeScript codebase needs query-key-based inference for fetched and selected data.

interview.question: What problem does queryOptions solve?
interview.answer: queryOptions creates a reusable query configuration from options such as queryKey and queryFn. The returned object carries query-function data and error types through the query key, improving inference when reused.
interview.followUp: Why is that useful beyond hooks? The same options can be passed to imperative QueryClient APIs, so one definition can coordinate declarative and imperative access.

interview.question: What does queryOptions accept and return?
interview.answer: Its options parameter is a QueryOptions-shaped object, and queryKey is required. The function returns the corresponding options object with a typed query-key data tag.
interview.followUp: What must remain consistent when reusing it? The query key and query function should describe the same resource so cache identity and inferred data remain aligned.

interview.question: Where can the returned options be used?
interview.answer: A queryOptions result can generally be passed to useQuery and to imperative APIs such as queryClient.query. This makes the query definition reusable instead of duplicating its key and fetch behavior.
interview.followUp: How would you share a parameterized query? Create a function that accepts the parameter and returns queryOptions with that parameter included in queryKey and used by queryFn.

keyPoints: One options definition can serve both hook-based reads and imperative client operations.
The API is generic over query-function data, error, selected data, and query-key types.
When initialData is supplied, the resulting option type reflects defined initial data.
The query key identifies the cache entry generated by the options.
gotchas: A queryKey must be supplied; it is not optional.
The function accepts the normal useQuery option set, but the options still need to match the selected framework's API.

redirect.summary: TanStack Router's redirect function creates a Redirect object that can be returned or thrown to navigate from route callbacks. The throw option controls whether the object is thrown immediately.
redirect.explanation: TanStack Router's redirect function creates a Redirect object for changing location. Return it or throw it from callbacks such as a route's beforeLoad or loader; setting throw to true makes the function throw the object immediately.

parameters.name: opts
parameters.description: Options controlling the redirect behavior, including navigation properties and the optional throw flag.

redirect.returns: A Redirect object; it is thrown when the options object's throw property is true.

example.title: Redirect from beforeLoad
example.explanation: Throw the redirect from a route lifecycle callback to navigate unauthenticated users to the login route.

useCases.title: Redirect unauthenticated users from beforeLoad
useCases.scenario: Protecting authenticated routes

useCases.title: Abort a loader-driven route transition
useCases.scenario: Loading route data

useCases.title: Create type-safe relative redirects with Route.redirect
useCases.scenario: File-based routing

interview.question: What does redirect do?
interview.answer: redirect accepts one options object and returns a Redirect object by default. It can be returned or thrown from route beforeLoad and loader callbacks to trigger navigation.
interview.followUp: How can a caller force throwing behavior? Set throw: true in the options; otherwise the object is returned.

interview.question: Where can redirect be used?
interview.answer: The function is useful in route lifecycle callbacks, especially beforeLoad and loader. Throwing or returning the resulting Redirect causes TanStack Router to navigate to the target location.
interview.followUp: Why might beforeLoad be preferable for authentication? It runs during route loading, allowing the redirect decision before the protected route finishes loading.

interview.question: What advantage does Route.redirect provide?
interview.answer: File-based routes can use Route.redirect directly. That helper automatically supplies the route's from value, which enables type-safe relative redirects without manually providing the origin route.
interview.followUp: When is an explicit from value unnecessary? When using the file-based Route.redirect helper, because it derives from from the route path.

keyPoints: redirect produces a Redirect object representing the requested navigation.
Use the object from route beforeLoad or loader callbacks by returning it or throwing it.
Its single argument is an options object that controls the redirect.
With throw omitted or false, the function returns rather than throws.
File-based Route.redirect derives the origin route, supporting type-safe relative destinations.
gotchas: Setting throw to true throws the Redirect object; when throw is false or omitted, redirect returns it instead.

refetchInterval.summary: refetchInterval makes a query poll on a timer. Use milliseconds for a fixed schedule or a callback for state-dependent polling that can stop by returning false.
refetchInterval.explanation: Set refetchInterval to a millisecond number for continuous polling, or provide a function that receives the current Query and returns a millisecond interval. Returning false stops and clears the timer; polling operates independently of staleTime while an active observer exists.
refetchInterval.syntax: refetchInterval: number | false | ((query: Query) => number | false)

parameters.name: refetchInterval
parameters.description: Polling period in milliseconds, false, or a function receiving Query and returning milliseconds or false.

example.title: Stop polling when a job completes
example.explanation: Polls the job every two seconds until the returned status is complete, then stops the timer.

useCases.title: Fixed-interval polling
useCases.scenario: A dashboard needs periodically refreshed prices, metrics, or status data.

useCases.title: Conditional job polling
useCases.scenario: A background job exposes a status endpoint until it reaches a terminal state.

useCases.title: State-controlled polling
useCases.scenario: Polling should pause while a component lacks required input or is explicitly paused.

interview.question: What forms can refetchInterval take?
interview.answer: A numeric value is interpreted as a polling period in milliseconds, so the query refetches repeatedly at that frequency while it has an active observer. A function is evaluated with the current Query and must return either a millisecond period or false.
interview.followUp: How would you stop polling after a terminal response? Return false from the callback when query.state.data indicates completion; this clears the timer.

interview.question: How does refetchInterval interact with staleTime?
interview.answer: Polling uses its own schedule and is not governed by staleTime. Therefore, a query may remain fresh while refetchInterval still triggers network requests.
interview.followUp: What should be changed if the requirement is freshness-based refetching rather than timed polling? Configure staleTime and the relevant refetch-on-event behavior instead of relying on refetchInterval.

interview.question: How can polling be made conditional?
interview.answer: The callback receives the Query object, allowing the interval to depend on current query state. It can return false to pause polling or a positive millisecond value to continue it.
interview.followUp: Can polling resume after stopping? Yes. If a later query result makes the callback return a positive interval again, polling resumes automatically.

keyPoints: refetchInterval enables timer-driven query refetching.
A numeric setting defines the period in milliseconds and operates while at least one observer is active.
A callback can calculate a dynamic period from Query state or disable polling by returning false.
Polling can restart automatically when the callback once again produces a positive interval.
Separate timers still share deduplication for concurrent in-flight requests.
gotchas: A fresh query can still refetch on its polling schedule; staleTime does not disable refetchInterval.
Multiple components observing the same key create separate polling timers, even though simultaneous in-flight requests are deduplicated.
Return false when polling should stop; a later positive result resumes polling automatically if the query result changes.

replaceEqualDeep.summary: Returns the previous value when it is deeply equal to the new value; otherwise, it reuses equal nested parts from the previous value. This supports structural sharing for JSON-like data.
replaceEqualDeep.explanation: replaceEqualDeep compares a previous value with a new value recursively. It returns the previous value when the two are deeply equal; otherwise, it builds the new result while reusing deeply equal nested parts from the previous value, which supports structural sharing for JSON-like data.
replaceEqualDeep.syntax: function replaceEqualDeep<T>(a: unknown, b: T, depth?: number): T;

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: The previous value, whose deeply equal parts are reused.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: The new value.

parameters.name: depth
parameters.description: The current recursion depth. Past a depth of 500, b is returned as is.

replaceEqualDeep.returns: T — a if b is deeply equal to it, otherwise b with its deeply equal parts replaced by those of a.

example.title: Reuse unchanged nested data
example.explanation: Reuses the unchanged nested user object while retaining the new count.

useCases.title: Preserve nested identity
useCases.scenario: A query receives a freshly parsed response whose unchanged nested records should retain their old references.

useCases.title: Minimize structural changes
useCases.scenario: A cache or state update needs a new top-level result while avoiding needless replacement of equal subtrees.

useCases.title: Share JSON data structure
useCases.scenario: Recursive comparison of JSON-compatible query data should share unchanged branches.

interview.question: What does replaceEqualDeep do when two values differ only in some nested fields?
interview.answer: It accepts a previous value and a new value, then returns the previous value when they are deeply equal. When they differ, unchanged deeply equal children from the previous value are reused in the returned new value.
interview.followUp: What happens with very deeply nested input? The documented recursion depth limit means that after depth 500, the new value is returned as-is.

interview.question: Explain the parameters and return type.
interview.answer: The first parameter is the previous value and may be unknown. The second parameter is the new value and determines the generic return type T; the optional third parameter represents the current recursion depth.
interview.followUp: Why can the first parameter be unknown? The function only requires it as a source of potentially reusable deeply equal parts, while the returned shape is typed from the new value.

interview.question: Why is this function useful in query-data processing?
interview.answer: It is useful for structural sharing between JSON values. Reusing unchanged references can preserve identity for unaffected subtrees and avoid treating those subtrees as changed.
interview.followUp: What should be considered before applying it to arbitrary data? The documentation specifically describes JSON values, so non-JSON structures should not be assumed to receive equivalent handling.

keyPoints: A completely equal new value produces the original previous reference.
For partially changed data, unchanged nested children in the new value are replaced with references from the previous value.
Its primary documented use is preserving shared structure across JSON-like values.
Parameter a supplies the references that may be reused.
Parameter b supplies the candidate result and its generic type.
The optional depth parameter records where recursive comparison currently is.
The return is either the old reference or a new-value-shaped result containing reused equal parts.
gotchas: The optional depth tracks recursion, and values deeper than 500 levels are returned without further structural sharing.

retry.summary: The retry option controls whether failed TanStack Query requests run again. It supports a retry count, disabling or infinite retries, and a callback for error-aware decisions.
retry.explanation: The retry option controls whether a failed query runs again. It accepts a retry count, false to disable retries, true for unlimited retries, or a function that decides from the failure count and error; client defaults are three retries, while server defaults are zero.
retry.syntax: retry: number | false | true | ((failureCount: number, error: TError) => boolean)

parameters.name: retry
parameters.type: number | false | true | ((failureCount: number, error: TError) => boolean)
parameters.description: Maximum retry count, false to disable retries, true for infinite retries, or a predicate receiving failureCount and error.

example.explanation: The query retries only twice for this error, then exposes the final failure.

useCases.scenario: A flaky network request should recover without immediately displaying an error.

useCases.title: Error-aware retry policy
useCases.scenario: Only selected errors should be retried while permanent failures stop immediately.

useCases.title: Client and server configuration
useCases.scenario: Different environments need different latency and resilience trade-offs.

interview.question: What forms can the retry option take?
interview.answer: retry may be false, true, a number, or a function receiving failureCount and error. false prevents retries, true retries indefinitely, a number limits retries, and the function returns whether another attempt is allowed.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid retrying authentication failures? Return false from the function when the error represents an authentication failure, and retry only transient failures.

interview.question: What are the default retry counts?
interview.answer: The client default is three retries, but server rendering defaults to zero. This avoids making server-side rendering wait through retry attempts unless the application explicitly opts in.
interview.followUp: Why might a server application configure retries explicitly? It may need resilience for transient upstream failures, while accepting the added rendering latency.

interview.question: How should a retry callback limit attempts?
interview.answer: The retry callback receives the current failureCount and the thrown error. Because the first retry attempt has a count of zero, a condition such as failureCount < 2 permits two retry attempts.
interview.followUp: How can retry timing be customized? Configure retryDelay with a number or function; a function can implement linear or exponential backoff.

keyPoints: A thrown query-function error triggers automatic retries until the configured policy stops them.
Retry behavior can be set globally or overridden for a specific query.
Use false when a failed request must immediately reach the error state.
A numeric value sets the maximum number of retry attempts before the final error is shown.
true enables unbounded retries, so it should be reserved for cases where that behavior is intentional.
A callback can choose retry behavior using both the number of failures and the error.
gotchas: A custom retry function must account for zero-based failureCount when limiting attempts.

RowModel.summary: RowModel is the processed table-row result used by TanStack Table. It provides hierarchical rows, flattened rows, and an ID-keyed row lookup.
RowModel.explanation: RowModel describes the result produced by TanStack Table's row-model pipeline. It exposes the current rows, a flattened version including sub-rows, and an ID-keyed lookup object for efficient row access.
RowModel.returns: An object with rows, flatRows, and rowsById collections.

type Person = { name: string }

declare const model: RowModel<Person>

const visibleRows = model.rows
const allRows = model.flatRows
const byId = model.rowsById

console.log(visibleRows, allRows, byId)

interview.question: What data does RowModel expose?
interview.answer: A RowModel contains rows, flatRows, and rowsById. The rows array preserves the hierarchical structure, flatRows removes nesting, and rowsById supports lookup by row ID.
interview.followUp: When would flatRows be preferable? It is useful when an operation must process every nested row as one flat collection.

interview.question: How does RowModel relate to table rendering?
interview.answer: The final row model is produced after the enabled row-model stages process the data. The documented pipeline can include filtering, grouping, sorting, expanding, and pagination before getRowModel returns the result.
interview.followUp: Why should rendering normally use getRowModel? Because it represents the final output after the applicable feature transformations.

interview.question: Why are three representations provided?
interview.answer: rowsById is an object keyed by row ID, enabling direct row retrieval without scanning the rows array. rows and flatRows serve hierarchical traversal and flattened traversal respectively.
interview.followUp: What determines whether nested rows appear in flatRows? The row model's generated sub-row structure; flatRows includes those sub-rows at the top level.

keyPoints: A RowModel deliberately offers three complementary views of the same processed data.
rows contains the row objects in their hierarchical arrangement.
flatRows is the convenient collection when nested rows must be handled uniformly.
rowsById maps identifiers to rows for direct access.
The ID map is intended for faster row lookup than repeatedly searching an array.
The final model can reflect a defined sequence of feature-specific transformations.
gotchas: For rendering, prefer the table's final getRowModel result rather than selecting an intermediate model yourself.

staleTime.summary: staleTime defines how long cached query data stays fresh. Increasing it reduces stale-driven refetches; Infinity waits for manual invalidation, while 'static' prevents even that from triggering a refetch.
staleTime.explanation: staleTime controls how long query data remains fresh after it is received. During that window, the cache can satisfy reads without stale-driven refetches; once it expires, normal background refetch triggers can apply. Infinity prevents staleness until manual invalidation, while 'static' also prevents manual invalidation from triggering a refetch.
staleTime.syntax: staleTime: number | "static" | ((query: Query<TQueryFnData, TError, TQueryData, TQueryKey>) => number | "static")

parameters.name: staleTime
parameters.description: Freshness duration in milliseconds, or the special value 'static'. A function form can compute the value from the query.
